summary: Defines a human-readable string form for LDAP search filters, which are otherwise sent over the network in a different encoding. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 2254.

eli5.summary: A short sentence that says exactly which entries you want from a directory, such as people named Smith in a certain place.

questions: how to write an ldap search filter
what is the ldap filter string format
how do ldap filter operators work
subtitle: A human-readable format for specifying which directory entries you want

tldr.problem: LDAP search filters are normally encoded in a binary format for transmission over the network, which is not readable by humans.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1960 defines a plain text format for writing LDAP filters using prefix notation with operators like &, |, !, and comparison operators =, ~=, >=, <=.
tldr.outcome: It was obsoleted by RFC 2254, which extended the format.

today: RFC 1960 was obsoleted by RFC 2254, which extended the format with additional features.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) defines network search filters that a client sends to a directory server to find entries. The RFC defines a human-readable string format so that filters can be written and understood by people, not just transmitted in their binary encoding.

The format uses a simple prefix notation: logical operators like & (and) and | (or) wrap other filters, and comparison operators like = and >= match attribute values.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing code that only computers understand, this format lets you write directory search rules in a way that people can read and write.

sections.title: The Filter Grammar
sections.content:
A filter is a parenthesized expression containing comparison operators. The equals operator tests exact matches, while approximately-equals tests similarity, greater-or-equal tests if a value is at least as large, and less-or-equal tests if a value is at most as large. The special syntax equals-asterisk tests whether an attribute is present. Substring matching uses asterisks as wildcards.

Logical operators combine filters. The AND operator requires all conditions to match. The OR operator requires at least one condition to match. The NOT operator inverts a filter. Complex expressions nest filters, for example matching entries with a name of John that also have an email address.
sections.eli5: It is like asking for records with conditional logic: find people named John with email addresses, or find all Smiths except Tim.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content: Simple equality: (cn=Babs Jensen) matches entries where the common name is exactly Babs Jensen. Negation: (!(cn=Tim Howes)) matches any entry except Tim Howes. Complex combinations like (&(objectClass=Person)(|(sn=Jensen)(cn=Babs J*))) match persons whose surname is Jensen OR whose common name starts with Babs J. Wildcards in values like (o=univ*of*mich*) use asterisks to match any substring.
sections.eli5: You can ask for people named John, or anyone EXCEPT named John, or people in New York with a phone number. The asterisk lets you match partial words.
